Returning from Khaibar, the Prophet marries Safiya, holds a wedding feast without meat or bread, and veils her, marking her as one of his wives rather than a slave.
At Khaibar the Prophet forbids donkey meat, as well as garlic and temporary marriage, has the pots overturned and allows horse meat; companions differ over the reason for the ban.
Khaibar's booty gives a horseman three shares and a foot soldier one; Banu al-Muttalib, called one with Banu Hashim, get part of its fifth, but Abd Shams and Nawfal none.
Abu Musa's party, whose boat took them to Ethiopia, reach the Prophet at Khaibar; he credits them with two migrations to Umar's one and knows the Ash'aris by their recitation.
Khaibar's booty: Abu Musa's late party get a share but Aban's none, a sheet stolen before division burns its taker, and Umar keeps conquered land undivided for all Muslims.
Abu Bakr refuses Fatima the Prophet's property, which the Prophet said is charity, not inheritance; after her death Ali, aggrieved at not being consulted, pledges allegiance to him.
Khaibar's governor must not swap poor dates for fewer fine ones; its Jews farm it for half the crop, Muslims finally eat their fill, and a poisoned sheep is presented.
When people criticise Usama bin Zaid's command, the Prophet says they once criticised his father's, who was fit to command and dear to him, as Usama now is.
Under the treaty the Prophet returns next year for a three-day Umrah, Muslims walking briskly to show strength; Hamza's daughter is given to her aunt, and he marries Maimuna.
At Mu'tah, Zaid, Ja'far and Ibn Rawaha lead in turn and are martyred, Ja'far wounded only in front; the Prophet weeps, forbids the women's crying, and Khalid breaks nine swords.
Usama kills a man at al-Huraqa who had said there is no god but Allah; the Prophet's repeated rebuke makes Usama wish he had embraced Islam only that day.
Salama bin al-Akwa counts seven or nine expeditions with the Prophet, including Khaibar, al-Hudaybiya, Hunain and al-Qarad, and more under commanders such as Abu Bakr and Usama.
Hatib's letter telling Mecca's pagans the Prophet's plans is intercepted; the Prophet accepts his excuse and spares him as a Badr veteran, and a verse forbids befriending Allah's enemies.
In Ramadan of the Conquest year the Prophet sets out fasting with ten thousand men, then breaks his fast publicly on the way, so travellers may fast or not.
Abu Sufyan, caught near Mecca, accepts Islam and watches the army pass; the Prophet recites Surat al-Fath on his camel, notes Aqil left no house, and orders Ibn Khatal killed.
Entering Mecca by Kada, the Prophet strikes the 360 idols round the Ka'bah, has its images removed before entering it, and prays eight rak'at of Duha at Umm Hani's.
In his bowings and prostrations the Prophet used to glorify and praise Allah, our Lord, and ask Him for forgiveness.
Umar asks the Badr elders and Ibn Abbas about the sura on Allah's help and the conquest; Ibn Abbas says it signals the Prophet's approaching death, and Umar agrees.
On the second day of the Conquest the Prophet declares Mecca a sanctuary from Allah where no blood may be shed nor trees cut, fighting allowed him only briefly.
In Mecca in the Conquest year the Prophet declares that Allah and His Messenger have made the selling of wine unlawful.
Staying in Mecca for ten or nineteen days, the Prophet and his companions shorten their prayers; Ibn Abbas shortens up to nineteen days and prays in full beyond.
Amr bin Salama recalls tribes awaiting the Conquest to embrace Islam and his leading their prayer as a boy who knew most Quran; two others met the Prophet that year.
At the Conquest the Prophet rules Zam'a's slave-girl's son, claimed for Utba, is Abd bin Zam'a's brother, for the child belongs to the bed, but has Sauda veil from him.
During the Conquest a woman steals; rejecting Usama's plea, the Prophet says he would cut even Fatima's hand, and hers is cut; she sincerely repents and later marries.
After the Conquest the Prophet takes pledges for Islam and jihad, not migration; Ibn Umar and Aisha say migration has ended, though jihad and intention remain, as Islam now prevails.
On the day of the Conquest the Prophet declares Mecca a sanctuary until the Day of Resurrection, where game is not chased nor plants cut, except idhkhir at al-Abbas's request.
Ibn Abi Aufa bears a Hunain scar; al-Bara says that when Hawazin's arrows routed the hasty, the Prophet did not flee but proclaimed himself the Prophet, son of Abdul-Muttalib.
When Hawazin's delegation, now Muslim, asks back their property and captives, the Prophet has them choose one, and the Muslims willingly return the captives, as their chiefs confirm.
Returning from Hunain, Umar asks about his pre-Islamic vow to perform I'tikaf, and the Prophet tells him to fulfil it.
At Hunain Abu Qatada gets the spoils of a pagan he killed; after Hunain Abu Amir is shot at Autas, and the Prophet asks forgiveness for him and Abu Musa.
While besieging Ta'if the Prophet bars an effeminate man from entering upon women; when the fort holds out, his companions fight and are wounded, then gladly agree to return.
Sa'd, first to shoot an arrow in Allah's cause, and Abu Bakra, who came over Ta'if's fort wall, report that knowingly claiming a false father denies one Paradise.
At al-Ji'rana a bedouin rejects the Prophet's good tidings, so Abu Musa and Bilal accept them and drink and pour on themselves water he had washed in.
At al-Ji'rana Ya'la sees the Prophet red-faced under revelation, after which he tells a man in Ihram for Umrah to wash off his perfume and remove his cloak.
The Prophet gives Hunain's booty to Quraish and new Muslims, not the Ansar, asking them to be content to take him home; faulted by a man, he recalls Moses' patience.
A detachment sent to Najd returns with thirteen camels each; Khalid kills and captures men of Jadhima who said 'Saba'na' instead of 'Aslamna', and the Prophet disowns what Khalid did.
An angry commander orders his troops into a fire; they hold back, and the Prophet says they would never have come out, obedience being due only in what is good.
Sent to govern Yemen, Abu Musa and Mu'adh are told to make things easy; the Prophet forbids all intoxicants, an apostate is killed, and they compare their Quran recitation.
Abu Musa, back from governing his people, took Ihram with the Prophet's intention but brought no sacrificial animal, so is told to do Tawaf and Sa'i and end Ihram.
Mu'adh is told to invite the People of the Scripture in Yemen to the testimony, then prayer, then Zakat; there he leads Fajr reciting that Allah took Abraham as Khalil.
